function.name: generate_image_tool
function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.name: tts_tool
function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

speaker.description: The voice to be used for the text-to-speech conversion.

file_name.description: The name of the file to save the audio output without the extension. If left empty, a default name will be generated based on the content.

function.name: write_markdown_tool
function.description: Writes the provided content to a Markdown (.md) file on the disk. This function should be used when there is a need to persist text data in Markdown format as a result of a user action or a process that requires saving information in a structured text file. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: write_html_tool
function.description: Writes an HTML file to disk with the given content. Ensures HTML tags within the content are properly closed. This function should be used when there is a need to save HTML content to a file as part of a 'save' operation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: search_web_tool
function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to launch a Google Compute Engine VM that has a single NVIDIA RTX A6000‑style GPU (the closest match in GCP is the `nvidia-tesla-a100` accelerator) and boots from the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image.

> ⚠️ **Important notes**
> * GCP does **not** use the “EC2” terminology – that’s Amazon Web Services. In GCP the service is called **Compute Engine**.
> * The RTX A6000 is a workstation‑class GPU. GCP currently offers the `nvidia-tesla-a100` accelerator, which is the next‑generation GPU that is comparable in performance. If you specifically need the RTX A6000, you would have to run a custom‑VM on a bare‑metal host or use a different provider that offers that exact GPU.
> * You must have a project with billing enabled, the Compute Engine API enabled, and the appropriate IAM permissions (`roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1` or higher).
> * The following examples assume you have the `gcloud` CLI installed and authenticated (`gcloud auth login`).

---

## 1️⃣ Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Variables
PROJECT="my-gcp-project-id"
ZONE="us-central1-a"          # pick a zone that supports GPUs
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-demo"
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8"  # 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM – adjust as needed
DISK_SIZE_GB=50
DISK_TYPE="pd-ssd"

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
    --project="$PROJECT" \
    --zone="$ZONE" \
    --machine-type="$MACHINE_TYPE" \
    --accelerator="type=nvidia-tesla-a100,count=1" \
    --image-family="ubuntu-2004-lts" \
    --image-project="ubuntu-os-cloud" \
    --boot-disk-size="${DISK_SIZE_GB}GB" \
    --boot-disk-type="$DISK_TYPE" \
    --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
    --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh   # optional: add a startup script
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU + RAM configuration |
| `--accelerator` | Adds a GPU; `count=1` means one GPU |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Selects the Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| `--boot-disk-size` & `--boot-disk-type` | Size & speed of the boot disk |
| `--maintenance-policy=MIGRATE` | Keeps the instance running during maintenance |
| `--scopes` | Grants the instance permission to use all GCP APIs (adjust if you want tighter scopes) |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script` | Optional: runs a shell script at first boot |

> 📌 **Tip:** If you want to use the newer `nvidia-tesla-a100` GPU, make sure the zone you choose actually supports it. Use `gcloud compute accelerator-types list --filter="name:nvidia-tesla-a100"` to see supported zones.

---

## 2️⃣ Using the REST API (HTTP)

If you prefer to call the API directly (e.g., from a script or a CI/CD pipeline), here’s a minimal **POST** request you can send to the Compute Engine endpoint.

```http
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/{project}/zones/{zone}/instances
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-demo",
  "machineType": "projects/{project}/zones/{zone}/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 50,
        "diskType": "projects/{project}/zones/{zone}/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/{project}/zones/{zone}/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100"
    }
  ],
  "scheduling": {
    "automaticRestart": true,
    "preemptible": false,
    "onHostMaintenance": "MIGRATE"
  },
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ]
}
```

### How to call it

1. **Get an OAuth 2.0 access token** that has the scope `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform`.  
   ```bash
   ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
   ```
2. **Send the request** (using `curl`, Postman, or any HTTP client):

   ```bash
   curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d @instance.json \
     "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/$PROJECT/zones/$ZONE/instances"
   ```

   Replace `@instance.json` with the path to a file containing the JSON body above (or embed the JSON directly with `-d '{...}'`).

---

## 3️⃣ Quick sanity check after creation

Once the instance is up, you can verify the GPU is visible:

```bash
# SSH into the instance
gcloud compute ssh "$INSTANCE_NAME" --zone="$ZONE"

# Inside the VM
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-470   # install drivers
nvidia-smi
```

You should see a table listing the NVIDIA A100 GPU (or the specific GPU type you requested).

---

## 4️⃣ Optional: Adding a startup script

If you want the VM to automatically install CUDA, cuDNN, or any other software on first boot, create a file named `startup.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
apt-get update
apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-470
reboot
```

Then pass it to the `gcloud` command with `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh`.

---

### Recap

| Tool | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| `gcloud compute instances create` | CLI command shown above | Creates the VM with GPU via the CLI |
| REST API POST | JSON body shown above | Creates the VM via HTTP (useful for automation) |
| `nvidia-smi` | Run inside the VM | Confirms the GPU is present and healthy |

Feel free to tweak the machine type, disk size, or GPU count to fit your workload. Happy computing!
